blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Unit 8 (Numerical Solutions of Nonlinear Equations (TOC: 'Numerical Method')), arranged by the unit's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation that shows the working.
8.1 Basic Principles of Approximating Real Roots of Nonlinear Equations

blocks.prompt: 1 A root (zero) of the function \(y = f(x)\) is a value of \(x\) for which:
blocks.explanation: A root of \(f\) is a value of \(x\) that makes \(y = f(x) = 0\), i.e. a solution of \(f(x) = 0\).

book_ref.quote: A root (or zero) of a function

blocks.prompt: 2 Geometrically, a real root of \(y = f(x)\) is shown by the point where the graph of \(f\):
blocks.explanation: A root is a common solution of \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = 0\); the line \(y = 0\) is the \(x\)-axis, so the root is where the graph meets the \(x\)-axis.

book_ref.quote: the geometric representation of a root of the function

blocks.prompt: 3 The graph of \(y = f(x)\) meets the \(x\)-axis at the point \((3, 0)\). Then a root of \(f\) is:
blocks.explanation: The root is the number \(x = 3\) (since \(f(3) = 0\)); \((3, 0)\) is the point on the graph.

book_ref.quote: Two ways of seeing the same root

blocks.prompt: 4 Which one of the following is a nonlinear equation?
blocks.explanation: \(x + e^{x}\) cannot be written as \(ax + b\) because \(x\) appears inside the exponential function. The other three are of the form \(ax + b = 0\).

book_ref.quote: the variable may appear with powers greater than one or inside trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic or other nonlinear functions

blocks.prompt: 5 The roots of \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2x - 8\) are:

book_ref.quote: A nonlinear equation is an equation of the form

blocks.prompt: 6 No general algebraic formula exists for the roots of polynomial equations of degree:
blocks.explanation: Formulas exist for quadratic, cubic and quartic equations, but none for quintic (degree 5) or higher-degree polynomials.

book_ref.quote: no general algebraic formula is available for quintic or higher-degree polynomials

blocks.prompt: 7 A linear equation \(ax + b = 0\) with \(a \ne 0\) has:
blocks.explanation: \(ax + b = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\frac{b}{a}\), one root only. It is the nonlinear equation that may have no root, one root or many roots.

book_ref.quote: May have no root, one root or many roots

blocks.prompt: 8 A true root is \(-2.4567\ldots\). Correct to two decimal places it is written as:
blocks.explanation: The third decimal is 6 (\(\ge 5\)), so the second decimal goes up: \(-2.4567 \to -2.46\). \(-2.45\) is cutting off, not rounding.

book_ref.quote: Always keep more decimals in your working (at least 4) and round only at the end.

blocks.prompt: 9 The Location of Root Theorem (LRT) can be applied to f on [a, b] when:
blocks.explanation: LRT: if \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and \(f(a)f(b) < 0\) (opposite signs), then \(f\) has a root in \(]a, b[\).

book_ref.quote: real-valued function which is continuous on a closed interval

blocks.prompt: 10 If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(f(a)f(b) < 0\), then in \(]a, b[\) the function \(f\) has:
blocks.explanation: The LRT guarantees at least one root; the curve may cross the axis three (or any odd number of) times.

book_ref.quote: The theorem promises one, not exactly one.

blocks.prompt: 11 Which one is an interval of sign change for \(f(x) = x^{3} - 6x + 2\)?

book_ref.quote: an interval of sign change for the function

blocks.prompt: 12 For \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}\), \(f(1) = -1\) and \(f(3) = 1\), yet \(f\) has no root in \(]1, 3[\). The reason is:

options.text: the LRT gives exactly one root

blocks.explanation: The LRT needs continuity on \([1, 3]\); \(\frac{1}{x - 2}\) is undefined at \(x = 2\), the graph jumps there, so the sign change proves nothing.

book_ref.quote: Continuity cannot be dropped.

blocks.prompt: 13 \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(f(a)f(b) > 0\). Which statement is correct?

options.text: \(f\) has exactly one root in \(]a, b[\)
The LRT gives no conclusion; \(]a, b[\) may or may not contain roots

blocks.explanation: Same signs at the ends do not rule out roots: e.g. \((x - 1)(x - 2)\) is \(2\) at \(x = 0\) and at \(x = 3\) but has roots \(1, 2\) in between.

book_ref.quote: No sign change does not mean no root.

blocks.explanation: The sign flips on \([-4, -2]\), \([-2, 0]\), \([0, 2]\) and \([2, 4]\): four separate intervals of sign change, so at least 4 roots (they are \(\pm 1, \pm 3\)).

book_ref.quote: Separate (non-overlapping) intervals of sign change give separate roots

blocks.prompt: 15 For \(f(x) = x^{3} + x - 5\), the value of \(f(1)f(2)\) and the conclusion are:
blocks.explanation: \(f(1) = 1 + 1 - 5 = -3\), \(f(2) = 8 + 2 - 5 = 5\); \(f(1)f(2) = -15 < 0\) and \(f\) is a continuous polynomial, so by the LRT a root lies in \(]1, 2[\).

book_ref.quote: A product is negative only when one factor is negative and the other positive

blocks.prompt: 16 A continuous function has \(f(2) = -3\) and \(f(5) = 4\). Which must be true?
blocks.explanation: \(f(2)f(5) = -12 < 0\) and \(f\) is continuous, so the graph goes from below the axis to above it and must cross at some \(c\) in \(]2, 5[\); it need not be the midpoint 3.5.

book_ref.quote: its graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil from the paper

blocks.text: 8.2 Graphical Method for Approximating Real Roots

blocks.prompt: 17 The graphical method is mainly suitable for a root correct to:
blocks.explanation: A graph is read by eye, so the crossing can be read to only one or two decimal places; the numerical methods of 8.3 then improve it.

book_ref.quote: is mainly suitable for obtaining the root correct up to one or two decimal places

blocks.prompt: 18 In this unit the graphical method is mainly used to:

options.text: give a starting estimate for the Bisection, Regula-Falsi and Newton-Raphson methods

blocks.explanation: It gives a first rough estimate (one or two decimals) that the iterative methods then sharpen.

book_ref.quote: used to provide an initial estimate for numerical methods

blocks.prompt: 19 For \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\), \(f(1.4) = -0.04\) and \(f(1.5) = 0.25\). The graph of \(f\) crosses the \(x\)-axis between:
blocks.explanation: The sign changes from \(-\) to \(+\) between 1.4 and 1.5, so (by the LRT) the crossing lies in \(]1.4, 1.5[\); indeed \(\sqrt{2} = 1.414\ldots\)

book_ref.quote: within the interval of sign change only

blocks.prompt: 20 While tabulating \(f(x) = x - 2\sin x\), the value of \(\sin 0.5\) to be used is:
blocks.explanation: Calculus uses radians: \(\sin 0.5 = 0.4794\). \(0.0087\) is \(\sin 0.5^{\circ}\) (degree mode) and \(0.8776\) is \(\cos 0.5\).

book_ref.quote: always keep your calculator in radian mode

blocks.prompt: 21 For \(f(x) = 2x - e^{-x}\): \(f(0.3) = -0.1408\) and \(f(0.4) = 0.1297\). Treating the curve as nearly straight between these points, the root to two decimal places is about:
blocks.explanation: The curve rises \(0.1408 + 0.1297 = 0.2705\) over the step 0.1 and reaches 0 after \(\frac{0.1408}{0.2705} \approx 0.52\) of it: \(0.3 + 0.052 \approx 0.35\) (true root \(0.3517\)).

book_ref.quote: This method provides a visual way to locate where a function crosses

blocks.text: 8.3 Numerical Methods for Solving Nonlinear Equations

blocks.prompt: 22 Which methods start from an interval of sign change and keep the root trapped inside it?
blocks.explanation: Bisection and Regula-Falsi both need f continuous on [a, b] with f(a)f(b) < 0; Newton-Raphson starts from a single value x0.

book_ref.quote: Bisection and Regula-Falsi start from an interval of sign change

blocks.prompt: 23 Bisection, Regula-Falsi and Newton-Raphson are called iterative methods because:

options.text: they give the exact root in one step
each step takes an estimate and produces a better one, repeated until accurate enough
they need the graph of f

blocks.explanation: Iterative means the same step is repeated; each repetition improves the estimate until the tolerance is met.

book_ref.quote: each step improves the estimate of the root

blocks.prompt: 24 Which method needs the derivative of f?
blocks.explanation: Newton-Raphson uses the tangent: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\). Bisection and Regula-Falsi use only values of \(f\).

book_ref.quote: These methods use the concept of intervals where the function changes sign

blocks.text: 8.3.1 General Rule of Accuracy, Tolerance and Calculator Setup

blocks.prompt: 25 For a root correct to 3 decimal places, the stopping tolerance is:

book_ref.quote: is the number of decimal places required for the root

blocks.prompt: 26 For a root correct to 4 decimal places, the tolerance is:

book_ref.quote: we will follow the function value criterion

blocks.prompt: 27 To obtain a root correct to 2 decimal places, the least number of decimal places the calculator should be fixed to during the working is:
blocks.explanation: Fix at least \(n + 1 = 3\) decimal places in the intermediate work, and round only the final answer to 2.

book_ref.quote: decimal places through all the intermediate calculations and round the final answer to the required accuracy

blocks.prompt: 28 Which value of \(|f(c)|\) allows us to stop for a root correct to 2 decimal places?

book_ref.quote: can move a number by at most half a unit of the last place

blocks.prompt: 29 For one decimal place (\(n = 1\)) the tolerance \(\frac{10^{-n}}{2}\) equals:

book_ref.quote: Use radian mode if trigonometric functions are involved.

blocks.prompt: 30 In the bisection method on \([1.2, 2]\), the first estimate of the root is:

book_ref.quote: The method systematically halves the interval to narrow down the location of the root

blocks.prompt: 31 In a bisection step \(f(a) < 0\), \(f(b) > 0\) and \(f(c) > 0\) at the midpoint \(c\). The next interval is:
blocks.explanation: \(f(a)f(c) < 0\), so the sign change (and a root) is in \([a, c]\): set \(b = c\).

book_ref.quote: How to decide which half to keep: look only at signs.

blocks.prompt: 32 Bisection on \(f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1\) over \([0, 1]\): \(f(0.5) = -0.375\). The interval for the next step is:

book_ref.quote: a simple and reliable numerical technique to find roots of nonlinear equations in one variable

blocks.prompt: 33 Bisection starts on \([0, 1]\). After 6 halvings, the length of the interval containing the root is:
blocks.explanation: After \(k\) steps the length is \(\frac{b - a}{2^{k}} = \frac{1}{2^{6}} = \frac{1}{64}\).

book_ref.quote: After \(k\) steps the interval has length

blocks.prompt: 34 Bisection on \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - 5\) over \([2, 3]\) gives \(f(2.5) = 5.625\). The second midpoint is:

book_ref.quote: Repeat Steps 2–3 until \(|f(c)|\) is near zero.
That is why bisection always works, but slowly.

blocks.prompt: 36 Starting on \([1, 2]\), the least number of bisection steps that makes the interval length less than \(0.01\) is:

book_ref.quote: It always converges, but slowly: the interval only halves at each step.

blocks.prompt: 37 The Regula-Falsi estimate of the root in [a, b] is:
blocks.explanation: It is the \(x\)-intercept of the secant line: each end point is multiplied by \(f\) at the other end. \(\frac{a + b}{2}\) is the bisection midpoint.

book_ref.quote: using the Regula-Falsi formula

blocks.prompt: 38 In the Regula-Falsi method the new estimate c is the point where the x-axis is cut by:

options.text: the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b))
the vertical line at the midpoint

blocks.explanation: Regula-Falsi joins the end points by a straight line (secant) and takes its x-intercept.

book_ref.quote: The idea of Regula-Falsi is to approximate the root by drawing a straight line through the points

blocks.prompt: 39 The slope of the secant line through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\) is:
blocks.explanation: Slope = change in \(y\) over change in \(x\) = \(\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\).

book_ref.quote: Slope of the secant line passing through the points

blocks.prompt: 40 The first Regula-Falsi estimate for \(f(x) = x^{2} - 3\) on \([1, 2]\) is:

book_ref.quote: Bisection and Regula-Falsi differ only in Step 2

blocks.prompt: 41 The first Regula-Falsi estimate for \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - 5\) on \([2, 3]\) is:

book_ref.quote: Write negative values in brackets when substituting

blocks.prompt: 42 The first Regula-Falsi estimate for \(f(x) = x^{3} - 5x + 1\) on \([0, 1]\) is:

book_ref.quote: the secant takes this into account, the midpoint does not

blocks.prompt: 43 For \(f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1\) on \([0, 1]\), \(f(0) = -1\) and \(f(1) = 1\). The first Regula-Falsi estimate is:
blocks.explanation: \(c = \frac{(0)(1) - (1)(-1)}{1 - (-1)} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\). When \(f(a) = -f(b)\) the secant cuts exactly at the midpoint.

book_ref.quote: Often one end never moves

blocks.prompt: 44 Compared with the bisection method, the Regula-Falsi method:

options.text: is usually faster, but also keeps the root inside an interval of sign change
never keeps the root in an interval

blocks.explanation: Both trap the root by sign change; Regula-Falsi uses the secant's x-intercept instead of the midpoint, which usually lands closer to the root.

book_ref.quote: It is usually faster than bisection

blocks.prompt: 45 The Newton-Raphson formula is:
blocks.explanation: Setting \(y = 0\) in the tangent \(y - f(x_n) = f'(x_n)(x - x_n)\) gives \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\) (minus sign).

book_ref.quote: This method works by drawing a tangent to the curve

blocks.prompt: 46 The tangent to \(y = f(x)\) at \((x_0, f(x_0))\) used in the Newton-Raphson method is:
blocks.explanation: The slope is \(f'(x_0)\) and the line passes through \((x_0, f(x_0))\): point-slope form.

book_ref.quote: The slope of the tangent line to the curve

blocks.prompt: 47 For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 12x + 1\), at which starting value does the Newton-Raphson formula break down?
blocks.explanation: \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 12\); \(f'(2) = 0\) (horizontal tangent, division by zero). \(f'(0) = -12\), \(f'(1) = -9\), \(f'(3) = 15\) are non-zero.

book_ref.quote: should not be zero near the root

blocks.prompt: 48 Newton-Raphson for \(f(x) = x^{2} - 3\) with \(x_0 = 2\) gives \(x_1 =\)

book_ref.quote: A zero slope means a horizontal tangent, which never meets the x-axis

blocks.prompt: 49 Applied to \(f(x) = x^{2} - 7\), the Newton-Raphson formula simplifies to:

book_ref.quote: Repeating this process produces a sequence of

blocks.prompt: 50 For the cube root of 7 we solve \(f(x) = x^{3} - 7 = 0\). The Newton-Raphson formula becomes:

book_ref.quote: the number of correct decimals roughly doubles at each step

blocks.prompt: 51 Newton-Raphson for \(f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1\) with \(x_0 = 1\) gives \(x_1 =\)

book_ref.quote: This tangent intersects the

blocks.prompt: 52 To solve \(e^{x} = 3x\) by Newton-Raphson from \(x_0 = 0\), the value of \(x_1\) is:

book_ref.quote: Write the given equation in the form

blocks.prompt: 53 Which statement about the Newton-Raphson method is correct?

options.text: It always keeps the root between two end points
A poor starting value can lead away from the root, because the root is not trapped in an interval
It does not need the derivative of f
It is always slower than bisection

blocks.explanation: Newton-Raphson starts from one value and follows tangents; it is usually fastest, but with a bad x0 it may run away.

book_ref.quote: This method does not rely directly on the Location of Root Theorem (LRT).

blocks.prompt: 54 Newton-Raphson for \(f(x) = \cos x - 2x\) with \(x_0 = 0\) gives \(x_1 =\)

book_ref.quote: Unlike bisection and Regula-Falsi, the root is not trapped in an interval

blocks.text: 8.4 Estimating the Value of a Definite Integral

blocks.prompt: 55 Which definite integral cannot be evaluated by elementary methods and is estimated numerically?
blocks.explanation: \(\sin(x^{2})\) has no elementary antiderivative. The others: \(x\sin(x^{2})\) and \(2xe^{x^{2}}\) by substitution \(u = x^{2}\), and \(e^{x}\) directly.

book_ref.quote: definite integrals are not always easy to evaluate analytically

blocks.prompt: 56 For a positive continuous function \(f\), the value \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx\) represents:

options.text: the slope of the curve at x = a
a root of f in [a, b]
the area between the curve and the x-axis from x = a to x = b

blocks.explanation: The definite integral of a positive continuous function is the area under its graph; this area always has a definite value even if no formula for the antiderivative exists.

book_ref.quote: The integral itself still exists.

blocks.prompt: 57 \([1, 3]\) is divided into \(n = 8\) equal subintervals. The width \(h\) is:

book_ref.quote: for some positive integer \(n\). Divide the interval

blocks.prompt: 58 For \(\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx\) with \(h = 0.4\), the number of subintervals and of points are:

book_ref.quote: Counting points as subintervals

blocks.prompt: 59 The Trapezium Rule states:
blocks.explanation: Adding the \(n\) trapezium areas \(\frac{h}{2}[f(x_{i-1}) + f(x_i)]\): end values once, inner values twice, all times \(\frac{h}{2}\).

book_ref.quote: is approximately equal to the sum of areas of the trapeziums

blocks.prompt: 60 The area of the \(i\)-th trapezium in the rule is:
blocks.explanation: Parallel sides \(f(x_{i-1})\), \(f(x_i)\), distance between them \(h\): area \(= \frac{1}{2}(\text{sum of parallel sides}) \times h\).

book_ref.quote: Length of the base of each trapezium is

blocks.prompt: 61 Using the Trapezium Rule with \(n = 2\), \(\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx \approx\)
blocks.explanation: \(h = 1\): \(\frac{1}{2}[0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3\). (\(\frac{8}{3}\) is the exact value; \(6\) comes from using \(h\) instead of \(\frac{h}{2}\).)

book_ref.quote: each trapezium approximates the signed area

blocks.prompt: 62 For a curve that bends upwards (like \(y = x^{2}\) or \(y = e^{x}\)), the Trapezium Rule:
blocks.explanation: The top of each trapezium is a chord, which lies above a concave-up curve, so the sum is too big (e.g. 3 against the exact \(\frac{8}{3}\) for \(\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx\)).

book_ref.quote: the chord lies above the curve and the rule overestimates

blocks.prompt: 63 The Trapezium Rule with \(n = 2\) gives \(\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{x}\,dx \approx\)
blocks.explanation: \(h = 0.5\), values \(1, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{2}\): \(\frac{0.5}{2}[1 + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{1}{2}] = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{17}{6} = \frac{17}{24}\). A larger \(n\) brings it closer to \(\ln 2\).

book_ref.quote: the accuracy of the approximation improves as n is taken sufficiently large

blocks.prompt: 64 For the Trapezium Rule on \([2, 4]\) with \(n = 5\), the point \(x_3\) is:

book_ref.quote: should be rounded to at least four decimal places to maintain accuracy in the final result

blocks.prompt: 65 A model gives \(2e^{-x} = x\). Before applying a numerical method we write it as:
blocks.explanation: Bring every term to one side: \(2e^{-x} - x = 0\) (or \(x - 2e^{-x} = 0\)); then find the root of \(f\).

book_ref.quote: bring every term to one side

blocks.prompt: 66 An equilibrium concentration satisfies \(xe^{2x} = 1\). For Newton-Raphson with \(f(x) = xe^{2x} - 1\), \(f'(x)\) is:
blocks.explanation: Product rule: \((x)'e^{2x} + x(e^{2x})' = e^{2x} + 2xe^{2x}\); the constant \(-1\) gives 0.

book_ref.quote: the equilibrium concentration or the reaction rate leads to nonlinear equations

blocks.prompt: 67 A signal model is \(x^{3} - 2x - 2 = 0\). Bisection on \([1, 2]\) gives \(f(1.5) = -1.625\). The next interval is:

book_ref.quote: The variation of these signals over time can often be modelled by nonlinear equations.

blocks.prompt: 68 A component voltage satisfies \(\sin V - 0.6V = 0\). Which value is the obvious (trivial) root that we do not want?

book_ref.quote: often produce nonlinear voltage-current relationships

blocks.prompt: 69 A key parameter satisfies \(x^{5} - 4x + 1 = 0\). Which is an interval of sign change for it?

book_ref.quote: involve high-degree nonlinear equations to generate secure keys

blocks.prompt: 70 Why is \(x^{5} - 4x + 1 = 0\) solved by a numerical method?

options.text: No general algebraic formula exists for degree-five equations

blocks.explanation: There is no general formula for quintic equations, so the root is approximated numerically (f(0) = 1 and f(1) = -2 show a real root in [0, 1]).

book_ref.quote: involve high-degree nonlinear equations to generate secure keys
